facts.text: Goliad is celebrated as the birthplace of Texas ranching, a legacy that still shapes the region’s identity.
The 1836 Goliad massacre, a pivotal moment in the Texas Revolution, is remembered as a turning point in the fight for independence.
Presidio La Bahía and its mission were relocated to the San Antonio River in 1749, establishing the first Spanish settlement in the area.
The Cart War Oak, also known as the Hanging Tree, still stands on the courthouse lawn and witnessed both sanctioned and unsanctioned executions during the Texas Revolution.
In 1976, Goliad’s downtown square earned a place on the National Register of Historic Places, preserving its historic streetscape.
Goliad sits on the Southern Pacific Railroad and the San Antonio River, linking it historically to regional trade and transportation.
